row.note: The commentary assigns the pasture’s drying to the same Lord who brought it out; Isaiah says the LORD’s breath dries grass and wilts its flower, making the agency explicit.
After grass and flower wither, Isaiah says God’s word stands forever; this sharpens the commentary’s sequence from vanishing pasture to the recitation promised not to be forgotten in 87:6.
The commentary hears guthā as debris carried off and later as what is discarded; Psalm 1 calls the wicked chaff that wind drives away, making the residue an image of judgment.

row.basis: grass grows then dries in a day
row.note: The commentary compresses pasture’s emergence and drying into one turn; this verse pictures morning growth and evening fading and drying, giving that short life a human-scale temporal image.
The commentary connects withered pasture to people who deny resurrection and become debris; this verse compares human days to grass and its flower, extending the plant’s transience to human life.
The commentary describes guthā as carried away and no longer counted; here wind passes over the flower, it is gone, and its place no longer knows it, closely specifying disappearance.

row.basis: green tree dried, dry tree made green
row.note: The commentary says the same divine hand brings out pasture and turns it to withered debris; Ezekiel says the LORD can dry a green tree and make a dry tree flourish, explicitly reversing both directions.

row.basis: a plant appointed to grow over Jonah
row.note: The commentary treats vegetation’s course as one of the Lord’s successive acts; in Jonah the LORD appoints a plant and makes it grow over Jonah, setting up a divinely governed plant life-cycle.
The commentary’s pasture is changed by its original giver; Jonah’s plant is struck by a divinely appointed worm and withers, so the same narrative names the giver’s action in a plant’s loss.
The commentary hears drying as the next act after growth; Jonah adds scorching east wind and the sun, and the plant’s death makes the change bodily and immediate for Jonah.

The commentary develops guthā as floating plant debris, pot foam, and something that disappears without being counted; Hosea places chaff blown from a threshing floor beside morning dew and smoke that vanishes.
The commentary links debris to the rejected side of choosing and sorting; Proverbs pictures a king winnowing the wicked and passing the wheel over them, making separation an enacted judgment.

row.basis: chaff swept away with no trace
row.note: The commentary says the debris is carried off and leaves nothing anyone counts; Daniel’s image has chaff swept away by wind until no place is found for it, adding total erasure.
The commentary joins floating debris, foam, dispersal, and forgottenness; Wisdom compares the ungodly’s hope to storm-driven froth and smoke, then to a guest’s unremembered stay.
The commentary’s guthā can be the rejected residue in a sorting scene; John’s image has a winnower gather wheat into the barn and burn the chaff, making the distinction eschatological.
The commentary reads the dark debris as pasture’s transient end; Peter quotes Isaiah’s grass and flower as the image of mortal glory, applying plant withering to human life.

Peter follows the withering grass quotation with the Lord’s enduring word; this closely meets the commentary’s juxtaposition of carried-off vegetation and the recitation that will not be forgotten in 87:6.
The commentary describes pasture changing into dry debris; James says a hot wind withers grass and its flower falls, using the plant’s sudden collapse to portray the rich person’s fading glory.

The commentary holds drying and pasture’s prior green life in one plant; Jesus uses a grain that falls into earth and dies before bearing much fruit, giving plant death a generative reading alongside the withering one.

row.basis: sown seed must die to live
row.note: The commentary connects plant emergence and decay with human return from earth; Paul answers a question about resurrection by saying what is sown must die before it comes to life, making the plant cycle an analogy for bodily resurrection.

The commentary develops dried vegetation as loose, useless matter carried away; Jesus pictures a branch that does not remain in the vine drying, being gathered, and burned, adding a relational and judgment reading.

row.basis: tree by water with unwithered leaf
row.note: The commentary imagines water held in hollows while surface debris goes; Psalm 1 contrasts wind-blown chaff with a tree planted beside water whose leaf does not wither, making rooted retention the other side of the image.

The commentary connects plant drying and renewal with the claim that humans too can be brought out of earth; Job says a tree may bud again at the scent of water, supplying a concrete plant-renewal image.

row.basis: human does not rise like a tree
row.note: The commentary uses the plant’s emergence from earth as a sign for human resurrection; Job’s lament says a human lies down and does not rise, preserving the contrary distinction between plant renewal and human fate.

The commentary holds darkened pasture’s former green within its final color and contrasts debris with retained water; Jeremiah’s tree by water keeps a green leaf despite heat, offering the enduring green counterpart.

row.basis: earth brings forth vegetation by command
row.note: The commentary treats pasture’s emergence as the Lord’s act before its transformation; Genesis begins plant life with God’s command that earth bring forth seed-bearing vegetation, locating growth within divine creation.
The commentary insists that mer'ā is pasture because animals eat it; Moses promises grass in the fields for livestock, making the pasture’s use and its giver explicit.

row.basis: grass for cattle and plants for people
row.note: The commentary identifies the emerging pasture as provision for grazing animals; the psalm says God causes grass to grow for cattle and plants for human use, linking vegetation to divine sustenance.
The commentary’s guthā is uprooted and swept along by water; the psalm says God sweeps people away like a flood before comparing life to grass, joining water’s force to transience.
The commentary contrasts debris carried on the surface with water caught and retained; Isaiah promises water on thirsty land and streams on dry ground, framing water as the source of restored growth.
The commentary remembers green pasture beneath the darkened debris; Isaiah pictures descendants sprouting among grass like willows by streams, giving the green stage a renewal and abundance reading.

The commentary sets what a flood carries away against hollows that hold its water; the psalm says God turns wilderness into pools and dry land into springs, a direct reversal from barren to water-filled.

The commentary describes pasture as food-bearing growth before its decline; after dry country becomes springs, this psalm has people sow fields and plant vineyards that yield fruit, showing renewal leading to provision.

The commentary contrasts floating residue with what remains held and green; Ezekiel’s river nourishes trees whose leaves do not wither and whose fruit continues, an image of lasting life sustained by water.

row.basis: God makes grass sprout in wasteland
row.note: The commentary treats emergence from dry earth as divine work; God asks whether he brings rain to desolate land and makes grass sprout there, extending agency to uncultivated ground.

The commentary says ahwā’s dark hue need not be ugly and recalls its use for beauty; the speaker calls herself dark yet lovely, giving a concrete literary instance where dark coloration and beauty coexist.

row.basis: straw distinguished from grain and true word
row.note: The commentary places worthless residue beside the enduring recited word; Jeremiah contrasts straw with grain while discussing what a prophet should do with God’s word, joining refuse-sorting to faithful speech.

The commentary links a plant’s withering to the denial of human return; Sirach explicitly maps falling and growing leaves onto generations that end and are born, making the plant-human analogy concrete.

row.basis: field grass alive today, burned tomorrow
row.note: The commentary treats drying pasture as part of the creator’s work; Jesus says God clothes field grass that lives briefly before being thrown into the oven, placing transience inside divine care.

row.basis: weeds gathered and burned, wheat stored
row.note: The commentary links the residue to what is rejected when the lasting is chosen; this parable has weeds gathered for burning while wheat is stored, giving the sorting image a final-judgment setting.
The commentary stresses pasture as useful feed before it becomes debris; Hebrews pictures land drinking rain and producing a useful crop, linking the land’s growth to blessing.
The commentary preserves the contrast between useful pasture and discarded residue; Hebrews sets thorn-bearing land against useful crop and says it is near a curse and ends in burning.

row.basis: rich person fades like a flower
row.note: The commentary extends withered pasture to people who prefer worldly life; James compares the rich person’s passing glory to a flower of the field, making the plant image a warning about status.

row.basis: seed differs from the body that grows
row.note: The commentary says the grass is changed in state rather than replaced by another object; Paul notes that what is sown is not the body that will be, preserving transformation and discontinuity in the seed image.

row.basis: God gives each seed its body
row.note: The commentary emphasizes the same creator’s successive acts over vegetation; Paul says God gives each seed the body he chooses, connecting plant transformation and divine agency.

The commentary sets withered pasture beside the next ayah’s recitation; Moses asks that his teaching fall as rain and his speech as dew on grass, joining authoritative speech to the plant’s source of life.
The commentary compares the pasture’s brief cycle with a preserved recitation; Isaiah says rain waters earth and makes it sprout before comparing that action to God’s effective word.

The commentary places the withering pasture beside a word that will not be forgotten; Isaiah says the word from God’s mouth will not return empty, completing its rain-and-growth analogy with durable efficacy.

row.basis: seed sprouts through night and day
row.note: The commentary says this ayah compresses a season into one immediate step, while Mark’s farmer sleeps and rises night and day as seed sprouts and grows by a process he does not know.

row.basis: stages from blade to ripe grain
row.note: The commentary contrasts its single fe with a longer sequence of growth and drying; Mark names successive stages from stalk to full grain before harvest, supplying a precise gradual counter-image.

The commentary turns the plant’s withering into an image for people who choose the transient world; this verse says evildoers soon wither like grass and fade like green herbs, making the moral application explicit.

The commentary’s guthā is plant matter swept away and no longer counted; Isaiah says all wither like a leaf and their iniquities carry them away like wind, adding a moral account of that disappearance.
The commentary sets floating debris against hollows that retain floodwater; Job asks whether papyrus or reeds can grow without marsh and water, making water retention a condition for plant life.
The commentary holds the green pasture within the darkened debris; Job says a plant can wither while still green and uncut, giving the color change a specific image of premature loss.

row.basis: root rots and blossom becomes dust
row.note: The commentary develops pasture turning into useless debris and being carried off; Isaiah likens judgment to fire consuming stubble, with a rotten root and blossom rising as dust, adding a moral cause and both plant parts.

row.basis: celestial agent makes each blade grow
row.note: The commentary assigns pasture’s emergence and drying to the same Lord; this midrash says each blade of grass has a heavenly constellation that strikes it and tells it to grow, adding an intermediary account of growth without denying divine rule.
The commentary describes guthā as uprooted vegetation that no longer holds to soil; in the sower parable a plant springs up, is scorched by the sun, and withers because it has no root.

row.basis: fruitless fig tree withers at Jesus’ word
row.note: The commentary frames pasture’s drying as a stage in the creator’s care; Jesus’ curse makes a leafy but fruitless fig tree wither, using plant death as a judgment sign rather than a seasonal passage.

row.basis: green wood contrasted with dry wood
row.note: The commentary traces green pasture into dry debris; Jesus uses the difference between green and dry wood to measure the severity of coming judgment, extending the plant contrast into a warning about human fate.

row.basis: God gives growth after planting and watering
row.note: The commentary emphasizes that the same Lord brings out pasture and transforms it; Paul distinguishes planting and watering by human workers from God giving the growth, adding a division of agency within cultivation.

row.basis: hay and straw among building materials
row.note: The commentary links guthā to the rejected, uncounted side of selection; Paul includes hay and straw among works built on a foundation, materials that cannot endure the coming test.

row.basis: fire tests and burns perishable work
row.note: The commentary compares transient vegetation with what lasts; Paul says each person’s work is disclosed and tested by fire, adding a judgment in which the work, rather than the person, is what burns.

row.basis: builder survives loss of burned work
row.note: The commentary’s ğuŝâ imagery can turn people themselves into debris; Paul distinguishes the person from combustible work, saying the builder may suffer loss yet be saved, a useful limit on the analogy.

row.basis: patient waiting for rain and harvest
row.note: The commentary contrasts the compressed fe with longer stages of plant growth; James pictures a farmer waiting patiently for the crop until the early and late rains, giving the growing season its slow human rhythm.

The commentary says withered pasture remains the same plant in a changed, useless state; Ezekiel’s vine wood is worthless for craft and is cast into fire as fuel, giving the loss of usefulness a judgment image.

row.basis: sealed spring in an enclosed garden
row.note: The commentary explicitly treats water-holding hollows as a secondary image beside floating debris; the Song’s enclosed garden and sealed spring offer a specific image of protected water, though its setting is erotic rather than a flood basin.

row.basis: well of living water and flowing streams
row.note: The commentary contrasts what a flood carries away with water retained in hollows; the Song names a well of living water and streams, a related water-source image without the commentary’s debris or flood scene.
